This also had penicilloyl specificity and was intensely reactive in skin tests, causing in one sensitized subject an alarming anaphylactic response in a scratch test.

evidence.experimental_conditions: intradermal injection
evidence.support_text: Penicilloyl polylysine (PPL), a penicilloyl conjugate, elicited wheal-and-flare skin-test responses in persons known to be hypersensitive to penicillin without stimulating production of reaginic antibodies.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Skin test dose of 10 µg of parent batches of standard B.P. and U.S.P. penicillin; three hypersensitive human volunteers.
evidence.support_text: Three volunteers, known to be hypersensitive to penicillin, tolerated therapeutic doses of batches from which the macromolecular proteinaceous residue had been removed but reacted to small skin test doses (10 µg) of the parent batches of standard B.P. and U.S.P. penicillin.

evidence.experimental_conditions: same patients as above (allergic to penicillin)
evidence.support_text: D-Penicillamine itself was unable to elicit a reaction in these patients, a fact which the authors attribute possibly to hapten inhibition by excess penicillamine. However, it may also be due to inability of penicillamine to form in vitro the multivalent conjugate necessary for reaction.

evidence.assay_type: human skin testing (intradermal or patch test inferred)
evidence.experimental_conditions: humans allergic to penicillin; conjugate prepared by treating HSA with penicillamine and potassium ferricyanide
evidence.support_text: Levine and Price (24) found that a small percentage of humans allergic to penicillin reacted positively to a multivalent penicillamine conjugate prepared by treating human serum albumin and penicillamine with potassium ferricyanide as oxidizing agent.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Therapeutic doses of batches from which macromolecular residue had been removed; three hypersensitive volunteers.
evidence.support_text: Three volunteers, known to be hypersensitive to penicillin, tolerated therapeutic doses of batches from which the macromolecular proteinaceous residue had been removed but reacted to small skin test doses (10 µg) of the parent batches of standard B.P. and U.S.P. penicillin.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 30% in oil/acetone; three daily epicutaneous applications on mouse ears; lymph node cell count by conductometry 24 h after last treatment
evidence.support_text: Penicillin G applied at concentrations up to and including 30% in oil/acetone did not cause any increase in ear thickness or lymph node cell count in the IMDS, indicating negative for sensitization.

evidence.experimental_conditions: intradermal test, drug concentration not specified
evidence.support_text: Patients sensitized to ABPC showed negative intradermal test reactions to PCG (penicillin G).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Guinea pig; non-maximized protocol; challenge on day 35 gave highest percentage
evidence.support_text: For penicillin G, the positive histological findings ranged from 25% for the Klecak (OET) test to 70% with the Magnusson & Kligman protocol.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 100 U penicillin G per 4 ml culture, 5 days incubation, 3×10^6 peripheral blood lymphocytes
evidence.support_text: No subject with negative immediate and negative delayed skin tests gave a positive lymphocyte response to penicillin G in the lymphocyte proliferation assay, indicating a negative response in those subjects.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 100 U penicillin G per 4 ml culture, 5 days incubation, 3×10^6 peripheral blood lymphocytes
evidence.support_text: Peripheral blood lymphocytes from ten patients with immediate skin test reactions to either penicillin G or penicilloyl-polylysine and from one additional subject with a positive immediate skin test but no adverse reaction, showed a positive lymphocyte response when cultured with penicillin G (100 U per 4 ml, 5 days). A positive response was defined as an increase of at least 5% reacting cells (large cells plus dividing cells) compared to negative control cultures.

Table 3 reports that 14 out of 43 patients with contact allergy to epoxy hardeners reacted to diaminodiphenylmethane (MDA/DDM) on patch testing, indicating a positive human skin sensitization outcome.
Table 3 reports that 2 out of 43 patients with contact allergy to epoxy hardeners reacted to ethylenediamine (EDA) on patch testing, indicating a positive human skin sensitization outcome.

Table 3 reports that 3 out of 43 patients with contact allergy to epoxy hardeners reacted to trimethyl hexamethylenediamine (TMD) on patch testing, indicating a positive human skin sensitization outcome.
Table 3 reports that 5 out of 43 patients with contact allergy to epoxy hardeners reacted to triethylenetetramine (TETA) on patch testing, indicating a positive human skin sensitization outcome.
Table 3 reports that 8 out of 43 patients with contact allergy to epoxy hardeners reacted to isophoronediamine (IPDA) on patch testing, indicating a positive human skin sensitization outcome.

3 of the 5 workers exposed to DEAEA developed allergic contact dermatitis from DEAEA, confirmed by patch test. DEAEA appears to be highly sensitizing, as 3 of the 5 exposed workers developed allergic contact dermatitis during the first 6 months following the start of exposure.
A case of an allergic reaction in a patient who had a positive patch-test reaction to titanium dioxide was recently reported, indicating titanium dioxide can cause allergic contact dermatitis.

Aalto‐Korte et al. in 2014 and 2015 reported Tris‐DMP (2,4,6-Tris dimethyl aminomethyl phenol) exposure as the potential cause for occupational contact allergy cases among construction worker painters in Finland (references 33, 34).

Allergic contact urticaria and asthma following direct hand contact with MDI glue was documented based on a positive MDI patch test, MDI-IgE, and MDI inhalation challenge (Valks et al. 2003). This provides direct human evidence that MDI skin exposure can induce contact hypersensitivity, a form of skin sensitization.

An allergic contact type dermatitis due to cutaneous sensitivity against the accessory photosynthesis pigment phycocyanin of Cyanoprokaryota (Anabaena sp.) was registered and confirmed by positive skin patch testing [193].
Contact dermatitis to lauramide DEA in shampoos was reported in a 73-year-old man with scalp psoriasis and eyelid dermatitis.
Contact dermatitis to undecyleneamide diethanolamide in a liquid soap has been described.

Fisher (1982) reported three patients who acquired an allergic contact dermatitis from the application of Cortaid cream containing the preservatives butylparaben and methylparaben; the three patients reacted to these parabens in patch testing.
In a large series of occupational contact dermatitis to plastics and glues from Finland, 3.1% of 360 patients patch tested were allergic to phenol-formaldehyde resin.

In a study during 1985-1992 on occupational allergic contact dermatitis due to cocamide DEA, 6 patients were allergic to this component. Additionally, contact dermatitis to cocamide DEA and lauramide DEA in shampoos was reported in a 73-year-old man with scalp psoriasis and eyelid dermatitis.
In a Swedish plant, six out of 88 workers developed contact allergy to phenol-formaldehyde resin.

Ketotifen was first recognized as a contact sensitizer in a Japanese cohort published in 1997. Reported cases to date are summarized in Table 1, which includes multiple cases from different countries where periorbital dermatitis or conjunctivitis was linked to ketotifen exposure, indicating positive human patch test results for ketotifen as a contact allergen.

Liden and coworkers [65] described 18 cases of toluene sulfonamide formaldehyde resin nail polish allergy; patch testing was positive to the resin in all cases, and dermatitis resolved after stopping nail polish use.

Tetrazepam, a benzodiazepine containing a cyclohexene ring, has been associated with allergic contact dermatitis confirmed by positive patch test in multiple clinical cases, including occupational exposures in nurses and pharmaceutical workers. Patch testing with various drugs showed positivity only to tetrazepam.

The other possible metabolites of styrene are 4-hydroxystyrene and 1-phenylethanol. The first of them shows positive contact allergic reactions when tested in the same study (63), but there was no conclusion about whether the proper compound or its epoxide was responsible for the reaction.

The paper states that 4-(4-hydroxy-4-methyl-pentyl)-3-cyclohexencarboxaldehyde (Lyral) is a 'well-known contact allergen' and that Myroxylon pereirae is a 'traditional contact allergen', indicating that human skin sensitization is established.

The paper states that numerous publications have documented cases of allergic contact dermatitis caused by methyl methacrylate (MMA), as confirmed by patch testing, and that several cases of allergic contact dermatitis in workers handling MMA have been recorded.

The table in paragraph 51 reports 10 patients with positive patch test reactions to mercapto mix in the occupational setting, and paragraph 53 reports 48 non-occupational positive reactions, indicating that mercapto mix causes allergic contact dermatitis (skin sensitization) in humans.
Triphenyl phosphate (TPP) demonstrated contact allergy on patch testing in a patient who developed contact dermatitis from a plastic facemask, which contained a similar allergen, triphenyl phosphite.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.02% aq. Methylisothiazolinone; European baseline series supplemented with baseline allergens
evidence.support_text: A 38-yr-old woman had ++ and + reactions to Methylisothiazolinone (0.02% aq.) in the European baseline series; facial sponge contained 387 ppm Methylisothiazolinone.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.1% aqueous amidoamine, patch test, 4913 patients
evidence.support_text: The NACDG evaluated 4913 patients for allergic contact dermatitis. Amidoamine (0.1% aqueous) was included. Positive results for amidoamine were observed in 2.3% of the patients.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.2% aq. Methylisothiazolinone; German baseline series
evidence.support_text: A 28-yr-old woman with history of atopic dermatitis had + reaction on day 2 and day 3 to Methylisothiazolinone (0.2% aq.) when tested with the German baseline series.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.2% Methylisothiazolinone aq. and 0.01% MCI/MI aq., 8 mm Finn chambers, Croatia, Nov 2015-Nov 2016
evidence.support_text: 798 patients: Testing in consecutive dermatitis patients with diagnosed Methylisothiazolinone contact allergy; Croatian baseline series included 0.2% Methylisothiazolinone aq. and 0.01% MCI/MI aq.; 13.2% (105) had positive reactions to Methylisothiazolinone.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.2% Methylisothiazolinone aq., Finn chambers, North America, January 2011-December 2014
evidence.support_text: 79 out of 9037 patients who had allergic reactions to allergens identified with wet wipes had 59% positive reactions to Methylisothiazolinone (0.2% aq.) in a retrospective review using North American Contact Dermatitis Group data from Jan 2011 to Dec 2014.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.2% Methylisothiazolinone aq.; Belgian baseline and additional series
evidence.support_text: A 60-yr-old nonatopic woman and a 36-yr-old atopic woman both had positive reactions to 0.2% Methylisothiazolinone aq. (+ and ++, respectively) and 0.002% MCI/MI aq. (++ each) following patch tests; household detergent contained 200 ppm Methylisothiazolinone.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.25% and 0.5% (w/w) concentrations applied via patch test
evidence.support_text: A 22-year-old female showed positive response in patch test to 0.25% and 0.5% (w/w) concentrations of a chemically synthesized hydrophilized ceramide resembling type 2 ceramide, indicating allergic contact dermatitis.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.5% petrolatum, Finn chamber, readings at D2 and D3, Chemotechnique Diagnostics allergens, according to ICDRG criteria
evidence.support_text: A 27-year-old non-atopic female with eyelid dermatitis was patch tested with multiple series; the only positive patch test was to coconut diethanolamide (0.5% petrolatum) with a ++ reaction at D2 and D3 according to ICDRG criteria. After removal of the shampoo containing this allergen, the dermatitis cleared.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% aqueous CAPB (possibly 0.3% active); patients provisionally diagnosed with cosmetic contact dermatitis
evidence.support_text: In 706 patients studied for skin allergy, 93 were provisionally diagnosed with cosmetic contact dermatitis; 4 of these 93 had positive reactions to CAPB 1% aqueous in patch testing.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% aqueous CAPB, patch test, 4913 patients
evidence.support_text: The NACDG evaluated 4913 patients for allergic contact dermatitis from January 1, 2001 to December 31, 2002. CAPB (1% aqueous) was included. Positive results for CAPB were observed in 2.8% of the patients.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% aqueous CAPB; patients clinically suspected of allergic contact dermatitis to cosmetics and toiletries; also tested with NACDG series
evidence.support_text: Fowler studied 210 patients clinically suspected of allergic contact dermatitis to cosmetics; patch testing with CAPB 1% aqueous gave positive reactions in 12 participants (5.7%), 7 of which were considered definitely relevant.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% in aqua, tested on patients with suspected allergic contact dermatitis
evidence.support_text: Formaldehyde (1% in aqua) showed a significantly increased age-standardized positive patch test rate of 3.6% in the medical occupations group (n=2234) compared to 2.1% in the control group (n=18964).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% in aqueous solution (aq.), applied to upper back, patches removed at 48 h, scored at 72 h
evidence.support_text: To pyrithione sodium (1% aq.) (sodium omadine) 1 out of 24 control persons showed a 2+ reaction. This positive reaction was considered allergic and relevant, possibly due to excessive use of antidandruff shampoos.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% w/w in petrolatum, Finn Chambers, occlusion for 2 days, readings at day 3 and day 7 (some patients not read at both)
evidence.support_text: Patch testing with DGEBA-R (1% w/w in petrolatum, Finn Chambers, 2 days occlusion) resulted in positive allergic contact dermatitis reactions in 15 out of 1299 patients, as per Table 1. One patient (no.14) reacted only to DGEBA-R and not to DGEBF-R. Reaction intensities ranged from + to +++ according to ICDRG criteria.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1.5% or 2% TDI (4.5e5 ng/cm² or 6e5 ng/cm²) in a modified European standard series; 360 dermatology patients tested for occupational skin disease
evidence.support_text: In a series of 360 dermatology patients skin tested for ACD to plastics and glues, 1.5% or 2% TDI (4.5e5 ng/cm² or 6e5 ng/cm²) was found to elicit an allergic response in only 0.8% of cases.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10 ppm Kathon
evidence.support_text: Subject 107-01 with atopic dermatitis showed a + reaction to Kathon at 10 ppm in patch testing.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10% benzoyl peroxide; occlusive conditions.
evidence.support_text: Poole (1970) reported a contact allergy confirmed in 40% of users (volunteers) under occlusive conditions with 10% benzoyl peroxide.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10% ethylene brassylate in EtOH:DEP; tested on 50 patients including 29 atopics with sensitive skin
evidence.support_text: In a patch test study of 50 patients including 29 atopics with sensitive skin, 10% ethylene brassylate in EtOH:DEP did not cause any positive reactions.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10% ω-pentadecalactone in EtOH/DEP, 50 µl, applied to backs, 48 h exposure
evidence.support_text: When 50 µl of 10% ω-pentadecalactone (EtOH/DEP) was applied to the backs of 50 subjects (38F; 12 M) for a 48 h exposure, one slight reaction of erythema was documented. Of these volunteers: 14 had allergic rhinitis; 11 had contact allergy; 5 had allergic asthma, food allergy, or drug allergy; and 4 had dermatitis atopic. Accordingly 58% of the subjects are atopics or characterized as sensitive skin.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 11 MI-allergic patients; 12 doses from 0.0105 to 60 µg MI/cm²; 15 µL on filter disc in Finn Chamber; occluded 2 days; readings on days 2, 3 or 4, and 7
evidence.support_text: In patch tests of 11 MI-allergic patients with 12 doses of methylisothiazolinone (MI), the lowest eliciting dose was 1.47 µg MI/cm² (49 ppm). No reactions were observed at 0.441 µg MI/cm² (15 ppm) or lower, and no reactions occurred in non-allergic control subjects.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 200, 500, or 2000 ppm Methylisothiazolinone, IQ chambers, France, Jan 2010-Dec 2015
evidence.support_text: 139 patients: Retrospective study of patients with Methylisothiazolinone-induced allergic contact dermatitis; relapses observed in 64% of patients and were severe in 18%.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 273 patients with personal history of atopy (eczema, asthma or hay fever); allergen is natural rubber latex (implied).
evidence.support_text: Correlation of prick and patch test results in 273 patients with a personal history of atopy: 8 had both prick and patch positive, 1 had patch positive with prick negative, totaling 9 positive patch test reactions to natural rubber latex.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 3,448 patients with occupational dermatitis tested for suspected glove allergy; study by Geier et al. 2012
evidence.support_text: In a study of 3,448 patients with occupational dermatitis due to suspected glove allergy, 3% were sensitized to mercaptobenzothiazole and/or its derivatives, indicating skin sensitization.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 3,448 patients with occupational dermatitis tested for suspected glove allergy; study by Geier et al. 2012
evidence.support_text: In the same study, 1% of patients were sensitized to MBTS only.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 33-yr-old atopic woman; patch test not specified
evidence.support_text: A 34-year-old atopic woman with immediate pain from eyelash extensions had +++ reactions on day3 to Methylisothiazolinone at 62, 250, and 2000 ppm, a ++ reaction at 125 ppm, and a + reaction at 31 ppm.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 4 patients with occupational allergic contact dermatitis from working with dental prostheses were challenged with EHMA via patch testing.
evidence.support_text: A small series of 4 patients that had developed occupational allergic contact dermatitis from working with dental prostheses were examined. All responded to challenge with MMA, but none displayed reactions following patch testing with EHMA (Kanerva et al., 1993).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 4 workers; patch test with N-phenyl-β-naphthylamine
evidence.support_text: Kobayashi and Saika (ref3) reported that in 4 workers using rubber product of dust-respirator mask, patch tests with N-phenyl-β-naphthylamine were positive in all 4 cases.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 5% concentration, human patch test on 1,606 consecutive dermatitis patients
evidence.support_text: β-Caryophyllene induced allergic responses in 10 (0.6%) of 1,606 consecutive dermatitis patients when tested at 5% in human patch tests.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 5% PG, patch test on 851 atopic patients
evidence.support_text: Allergic reactions were observed in 21 of 851 (2.5%) atopic patients patch-tested with 5% PG.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 62-year-old female; aluminum patch test with 94 eye cream components; readings at 48 and 120 h; isojasmone tested at unknown concentration
evidence.support_text: A 62-year-old woman developed acute contact dermatitis around her eyes. She had reported experiencing repeated allergic reactions to cosmetics and perfumes throughout her life. The patient was tested to the 94 individual components of her eye cream using the aluminum patch test. Reactions were read at 48 and 120 h. No reactions were observed to isojasmone (Larsen, 1975).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 96 h exposure on skin, 40 volunteers with various irritation and allergy susceptibilities
evidence.support_text: A patch test with soot with high content of SWCNTs showed negative results after testing for a period of 96 hours when performed in 40 volunteers reporting various irritation and allergy susceptibilities (Huczko and Lange, 2001).

evidence.assay_type: repeated open application test (ROAT) with deodorant

evidence.support_text: In a ROAT with deodorant, 8 dermatitis patients with prior patch test reactions to cinnamaldehyde were exposed to a deodorant containing 0.1% cinnamaldehyde twice daily for two weeks; 4 patients reacted (mid-dose).

evidence.assay_type: repeated open application test (ROAT) with deodorant
evidence.experimental_conditions: 8 patients with prior hypersensitivity to cinnamaldehyde; deodorant containing 0.32% cinnamaldehyde applied twice daily for 2 weeks
evidence.support_text: In a ROAT with deodorant, 8 dermatitis patients with prior patch test reactions to cinnamaldehyde were exposed to a deodorant containing 0.32% cinnamaldehyde twice daily for two weeks; 2 patients reacted (high-dose).

evidence.assay_type: repeated open application test (ROAT) with deodorant
evidence.experimental_conditions: 9 patients with prior hypersensitivity to cinnamaldehyde; deodorant containing 0.01% cinnamaldehyde applied twice daily for 2 weeks
evidence.support_text: In a second ROAT study with the same protocol, deodorants containing 0.01% cinnamaldehyde were tested in 9 patients with prior hypersensitivity; 1 out of 9 reacted to the low dose.

evidence.assay_type: repeated open application test (ROAT) with deodorant
evidence.experimental_conditions: 9 patients with prior hypersensitivity to cinnamaldehyde; deodorant containing 0.032% cinnamaldehyde applied twice daily for 2 weeks
evidence.support_text: In a second ROAT study, deodorants containing 0.032% cinnamaldehyde were tested in 9 patients with prior hypersensitivity to cinnamaldehyde; 4 out of 9 reacted to the mid-dose.

evidence.assay_type: repeated open application test (ROAT) with deodorant
evidence.experimental_conditions: 9 patients with prior hypersensitivity to cinnamaldehyde; deodorant containing 0.1% cinnamaldehyde applied twice daily for 2 weeks
evidence.support_text: In a second ROAT study, deodorants containing 0.1% cinnamaldehyde were tested in 9 patients with prior hypersensitivity to cinnamaldehyde; 3 out of 9 reacted to the high dose.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 15 ppm MCI/MI preserved lotion applied repeatedly in MCI/MI-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Frosch and Schulze-Dirks performed the ROAT in 7 MCI/MI-allergic patients, and showed that 4 (57%) reacted to 15 ppm MCI/MI preserved lotion and that 3 (42%) reacted to 9 ppm MCI/MI preserved lotion (177).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 7 ppm MCI/MI in a ROAT in MCI/MI-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Hannuksela et al. showed that 5 of 10 MCI/MI-allergic patients reacted to 7 ppm MCI/MI in a ROAT (178).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 9 ppm MCI/MI preserved lotion applied repeatedly in MCI/MI-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Frosch and Schulze-Dirks performed the ROAT in 7 MCI/MI-allergic patients, and showed that 4 (57%) reacted to 15 ppm MCI/MI preserved lotion and that 3 (42%) reacted to 9 ppm MCI/MI preserved lotion (177).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Double-blind provocative use test with skin lotion containing 15 ppm CMI/MI versus control preserved with parabens and DMDM hydantoin
evidence.support_text: Marks et al. performed a double-blind provocative use test with a skin lotion containing 15 ppm CMI/MI, versus a control preserved with parabens and DMDM hydantoin. Among 10 patients, 5 had positive reactions to the CMI/MI lotion alone, 4 were negative to both, and 1 reacted to the control lotion alone.

evidence.experimental_conditions: MI at 100 ppm in aqueous skin cream, applied twice daily for 2 weeks to outer upper arm, 25 cm² area, evaluated at baseline, 1 week, and 2 weeks
evidence.support_text: A repeated open application test was performed on 15 patients with known contact allergy to MCI/MI and/or MI. Each patient was given two sets of aqueous skin creams: one containing MI at 100 ppm and the other containing paraben preservatives. The creams were applied twice daily for 2 weeks to the outer aspect of the upper arm on an area of 25 cm². At evaluation after 1 and 2 weeks, 8 patients had positive allergic responses at the test sites that received the MI-containing creams.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 15 ppm MCI/MI in a lotion, applied twice daily for 1 week in double-blind placebo manner in 101 MCI/MI-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Furthermore, a European multicentre study including 101 MCI/MI-allergic patients was designed in a double-blind placebo manner to investigate the reactivity to 15 ppm MCI/MI in a lotion versus a lotion without MCI/MI (180). Patients were instructed to apply the lotions twice daily for 1 week, and 31% reacted to the MCI/MI-containing lotion, 3% to the placebo lotion, and 5% to both lotions.

evidence.experimental_conditions: product bubbling bath oil with 0.6% HCHO; applied twice daily for 21 days uncovered on right shoulder; subjects pre-screened as patch-test positive to 1% formalin (0.4% HCHO)
evidence.support_text: Subjects patch-test positive to 1% formalin were tested with a bubbling bath oil containing 0.6% HCHO applied twice daily for 21 days uncovered; 2/10 subjects showed skin reactions.

evidence.experimental_conditions: product dry skin lotion with 0.5% HCHO; applied twice daily for 21 days uncovered on right face and forearm; subjects pre-screened as patch-test positive to 1% formalin (0.4% HCHO)
evidence.support_text: Subjects patch-test positive to 1% formalin (0.4% HCHO) were tested with a dry skin lotion containing 0.5% HCHO applied twice daily for 21 days uncovered; 5/10 subjects showed skin reactions.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Daily application of lotion with 8.6 ppm MCI/MI to one elbow flexure for 1 week; other elbow flexure with lotion without MCI/MI; in MCI/MI-sensitized patients
evidence.support_text: Hjort and Roed performed use testing in 11 MCI/MI-sensitized patients (175). They were instructed to apply a skin lotion with 8.6 ppm MCI/MI daily in one elbow flexure, and a similar lotion but without MCI/MI in the other elbow flexure, for 1 week. No positive reactions were identified.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Daily exposure to 15 ppm MCI/MI in a lotion for 13 weeks in healthy volunteers
evidence.support_text: Schwartz et al. performed double-blind studies in healthy volunteers, in which subjects were exposed daily to either 15 ppm MCI/MI in a lotion or to a placebo lotion over a 13-week period (174). No evidence of dermatitis was found over the test period.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Lotion containing 15 ppm MCI/MI applied daily to elbow flexure for 1 week in MCI/MI-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Meneghini et al. performed a similar use test in 20 MCI/MI-allergic patients, although the MCI/MI content was 15 ppm in the lotions (176). They showed that 8 of 20 patients developed allergic contact dermatitis in response to the MCI/MI-containing lotion.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Soap with 0.05% ethylene brassylate for 6 months, then lotion with 0.03% for 3 months, then cologne products at 0.05%, 0.1%, 0.3%, 1% for 4 months; 75 subjects initially, 61 completed.
evidence.support_text: One elicitation study using ethylene brassylate as a negative control involved a 6-month use of a soap containing 0.05% ethylene brassylate, followed by 3-month use of a moisturizing lotion with 0.03%, and then 4-month use of four cologne products at 0.05%, 0.1%, 0.3%, and 1% by 61 subjects. No positive reactions due to ethylene brassylate were noted.

evidence.experimental_conditions: shampoo containing 0.02% MDBGN, used three times per week for 9-13 weeks, 12 MDBGN-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Tosti et al. challenged 12 MDBGN-allergic patients with shampoo containing 0.02% MDBGN three times per week for 9-13 weeks; none developed allergic contact dermatitis.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Overall concentration of 15% of the mixture (1:1:1) in shampoo
evidence.support_text: In a use test with shampoos containing a 1:1:1 mixture of geraniol, hydroxycitronellal, and 3 and 4-(4-Hydroxy-4-methylpentyl)- at an overall concentration of 15%, one patient with dermatitis history developed a visible skin reaction.

review_policy.eligible_subject: unique measurement-producing subject, donor, or cell-system species
